\proofstep
  {FABL.signMultiIndex_order}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p210-b002}
Let $Ω$ be a finite nonempty set with probability measure $π$, and let $ι$ be a finite
nonempty index set. Suppose $B$ is a basis of real-valued functions on $Ω$ that is
orthonormal for the $π$-weighted inner product and has a distinguished index $0_B$ whose
basis function is constantly one. For integers $n,k\ge 0$, suppose $f:Ω^n\to\mathbb R$
is a finite sum, over coordinate sets $J$, of functions each depending only on the
coordinates in its corresponding $J$, with every term indexed by a set of size greater
than $k$ equal to zero. Then the Fourier coefficient of $f$ at any multi-index whose
number of nonconstant coordinates is greater than $k$ is zero.
\end{theorem}

  {FABL.signMultiIndex_order}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p013-b007,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p210-b002}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty set, let $\pi$ be a probability mass function on
$\Omega$, and let $B$ be an orthonormal basis of real-valued functions on $\Omega$,
indexed by a finite nonempty set and containing the constant-one function as its
distinguished zero-indexed element. For a nonnegative integer $n$, let $f:(\mathrm{Fin}\
n\to\Omega)\to\mathbb{R}$ and let $k$ be a nonnegative integer. If every product-basis
Fourier coefficient of $f$ indexed by a tuple whose entries differ from the
distinguished index in more than $k$ coordinates is zero, then $f$ is a sum, over
subsets of the $n$ coordinates, of functions each depending only on the coordinates in
its indexing subset, with the summand equal to zero whenever that subset has more than
$k$ elements.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Spectral degree]
\lean{FABL.FiniteFourierBasis.spectralDegree}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p004-b006}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p036-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p215-b010
}
\label{FABL.FiniteFourierBasis.spectralDegree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteFourierBasis, FABL.FiniteFourierBasis.fourierCoeff, FABL.ProductL2, FABL.multiIndexOrder}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty set with probability mass function $\pi$, and let $B$
be an orthonormal basis of real-valued functions on $\Omega$ for the $\pi$-weighted
inner product, with one basis vector equal to the constant-one function. Let its index
set be finite and nonempty, and let $f\colon\Omega^n\to\mathbb{R}$. The spectral degree
of $f$ is the supremum of the orders of multi-indices with nonzero Fourier coefficient.
\end{definition}

  {FABL.FiniteFourierBasis.spectralDegree}
  {context}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p210-b002,

\proofstep
  {FABL.signMultiIndex_order}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p013-b007,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p210-b002}
Let $\Omega$ and $\iota$ be finite nonempty sets, let $\pi$ be a probability mass
function on $\Omega$, and let $B$ be a basis of real-valued functions on $\Omega$ whose
constant-one element is indexed by $0$ and which is orthonormal for the $\pi$-weighted
inner product. For a positive integer $n$, a function $f:\Omega^n\to\mathbb R$, and
$k\in\mathbb N$, the spectral degree of $f$ is at most $k$ if and only if every Fourier
coefficient indexed by a multi-index whose number of nonzero coordinates exceeds $k$ is
zero.
\end{theorem}

  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p210-b002,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p013-b007}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty set with probability mass function $\pi$, and let $B$
be a finite Fourier basis on $\Omega$ indexed by a finite nonempty set $\iota$. For
every function $f:(\Omega^n)\to\mathbb R$, its product degree equals its spectral degree
with respect to $B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Uniformity of a product distribution]
\lean{FABL.productProbabilityPMF_uniform}
\label{FABL.productProbabilityPMF_uniform}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.independentProductPMF, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{3}
Let $V$ be a finite set and let $D$ be a finite nonempty set. The independent product of
uniform distributions on $D$, indexed by $V$, is the uniform distribution on the set of
functions from $V$ to $D$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform product distribution on sign vectors]
\lean{FABL.productProbabilityPMF_uniformSign}
\label{FABL.productProbabilityPMF_uniformSign}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.productProbabilityPMF, FABL.productProbabilityPMF_uniform, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $n$, the product distribution of $n$ independent uniform signs
is the uniform distribution on the set of sign vectors of length $n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Support correspondence for binary multi-indices]
\lean{FABL.signMultiIndexEquivFinset}
\label{FABL.signMultiIndexEquivFinset}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.MultiIndex, FABL.multiIndexSupport, FABL.signMultiIndexSupport}
For each natural number $n$, the map sending a function
$a\colon\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\to\{0,1\}$ to the set of coordinates where it equals $1$ is an
equivalence between such functions and subsets of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Order of a Sign Multi-Index]
\lean{FABL.signMultiIndex_order}
\label{FABL.signMultiIndex_order}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.MultiIndex, FABL.multiIndexOrder, FABL.signMultiIndexSupport}
\difficulty{1}
For every $n\in\mathbb N$ and every multi-index $a:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{0,1\}$, its order,
defined as the number of coordinates where it is nonzero, equals the cardinality of its
support.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform sign mean equals cube mean]
\lean{FABL.productMean_uniformSign}
\label{FABL.productMean_uniformSign}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.mean, FABL.pmfExpectation_uniformPMF_eq_expect, FABL.productMean, FABL.productProbabilityPMF_uniformSign, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f$ be a real-valued function on the set of
sign vectors $\{−1,1\}^n$. Its mean under the product of uniform probability
distributions on the two signs equals its uniform mean over the sign cube.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Second moment on the uniform sign cube]
\lean{FABL.productSecondMoment_uniformSign}
\label{FABL.productSecondMoment_uniformSign}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.pmfExpectation_uniformPMF_eq_expect, FABL.productProbabilityPMF_uniformSign, FABL.productSecondMoment, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{3}
For every real-valued function $f$ on the sign cube $\{−1,1\}^n$, its second moment
under the uniform product distribution on that cube equals the uniform-cube expectation
$\mathbb{E}_x[f(x)^2]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform sign-cube variance identity]
\lean{FABL.productVariance_uniformSign}
\label{FABL.productVariance_uniformSign}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.pmfExpectation_uniformPMF_eq_expect, FABL.productMean_uniformSign, FABL.productProbabilityPMF_uniformSign, FABL.productVariance, FABL.uniformPMF, FABL.variance}
\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $n$ and every real-valued function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional
sign cube, its variance under the product of uniform sign distributions equals its
variance under the uniform distribution on the whole cube.
\end{theorem}

  {FABL.productMean_uniformSign}

  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p024-b002,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p026-b005}
For any two real-valued functions $f,g$ on the $n$-dimensional sign cube, their
covariance under the uniform product distribution on sign vectors equals their
covariance under the uniform distribution on the cube.
\end{theorem}

For every natural number $n$ and functions $f,g:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$, their product
inner product under independent uniform signs equals their uniform inner product, that
is, the average of $f(x)g(x)$ over all $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform sign coordinate projection]
\lean{FABL.coordinateProjection_uniformSign_apply}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p048-b007,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p212-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p212-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p213-b001
}
\label{FABL.coordinateProjection_uniformSign_apply}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.coordinateProjection, FABL.coordinateProjection_apply, FABL.finTwoSignEquiv, FABL.pmfExpectation_uniformPMF_eq_expect, FABL.replaceCoordinate, FABL.setCoordinate, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $i$ be a coordinate in $\operatorname{Fin}(n)$, and
let $f$ be a real-valued function on the sign cube $\{-1,1\}^n$. At each point $x$ of
the cube, the coordinate projection at $i$ is the average of the two values of $f$
obtained by setting coordinate $i$ to $1$ and to $-1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Coordinate projection as sign averaging]
\lean{FABL.coordinateProjection_uniformSign_eq_coordinateExpectation}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p049-b001,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p048-b007
}
\label{FABL.coordinateProjection_uniformSign_eq_coordinateExpectation}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.coordinateExpectation, FABL.coordinateExpectation_apply, FABL.coordinateProjection, FABL.coordinateProjection_uniformSign_apply, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $i$ be a coordinate in $\operatorname{Fin}(n)$, and
let $f$ be a real-valued function on the sign cube $\{-1,1\}^n$. The coordinate
projection at $i$ equals the operator that, at each point, averages the values of $f$
after setting coordinate $i$ to $1$ and to $-1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform product and cube total influence]
\lean{FABL.productTotalInfluence_uniformSign_eq_totalInfluence}
\label{FABL.productTotalInfluence_uniformSign_eq_totalInfluence}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.productInfluence_uniformSign_eq_influence, FABL.productTotalInfluence, FABL.totalInfluence, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{3}
For every real-valued function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional sign cube, its total influence
computed using the uniform product distribution on signs equals its total influence
computed using the usual discrete derivatives on the uniform cube.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform-sign coordinate noise]
\lean{FABL.productCoordinateNoisePMF_uniformSign}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p214-b005}
\label{FABL.productCoordinateNoisePMF_uniformSign}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.coordinateResamplingNoisePMF, FABL.productCoordinateNoisePMF, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{1}
Let $\rho\in[0,1]$ and let $x$ be a sign, that is, an element of $\{ -1,1\}$. The
coordinate noise distribution obtained by using the uniform sign distribution as the
resampling law is equal to the coordinate resampling noise distribution with parameter
$\rho$ at $x$.
\end{theorem}

  {FABL.signMultiIndex_order}
  {direct}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p210-b002}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\rho\in[0,1]$, and let $x$ be a sign vector of length
$n$. The product noise kernel on sign vectors, with the uniform distribution on signs as
its base distribution, equals the resampling noise kernel at correlation parameter
$\rho$ and input $x$.
\end{theorem}

  {FABL.productNoiseKernel_uniformSign}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p214-b005,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p053-b003}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $\rho\in[0,1]$. On the cube $\{-1,1\}^n$
with uniform measure, the product noise operator that retains each input sign with
probability $\rho$ and otherwise resamples an independent uniform sign agrees, on
every real-valued function $f$, with the Walsh noise operator: it multiplies the Fourier
coefficient indexed by a subset $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ by $\rho^{|S|}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Product noise stability on the uniform sign cube]
\lean{FABL.productNoiseStability_uniformSign_eq_noiseStability}
\label{FABL.productNoiseStability_uniformSign_eq_noiseStability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.noiseStability, FABL.noiseStability_eq_uniformInner_noiseOperator, FABL.productInner_uniformSign, FABL.productNoiseOperator_uniformSign_eq_noiseOperator, FABL.productNoiseStability, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\rho\in[0,1]$, and let $f$ be a real-valued
function on $\{-1,1\}^n$. Choose $X$ uniformly from the sign cube, and form $Y$ by
independently retaining each coordinate of $X$ with probability $(1+\rho)/2$ and flipping
it otherwise. The expected product $\mathbb{E}[f(X)f(Y)]$ equals the product noise
stability obtained by independently retaining each coordinate with probability
$\rho$ and otherwise resampling it as a uniform sign.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Influence of the two-coordinate indicator]
\lean{FABL.productInfluence_threePointBothCIndicator}
\label{FABL.productInfluence_threePointBothCIndicator}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteFourierBasis.productInfluence_eq_sum_sq_fourierCoeff, FABL.ThreePoint, FABL.productInfluence, FABL.threePointBothCIndicator, FABL.threePointBothCIndicator_fourierCoeff_table, FABL.threePointCIndicatorCoeff, FABL.threePointFourierBasis, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{5}
Let $X_0,X_1$ be independent and uniform on the three-point set $\{a,b,c\}$, and let
$F(X_0,X_1)$ equal $1$ when both coordinates are $c$ and $0$ otherwise. The squared
$L^2$ norm of the difference between $F$ and its average over coordinate $0$ is
$\frac{2}{27}$.
\end{theorem}
